posts.title: Safety-critical markets set the numbers
posts.excerpt: Drive-safety practice is written in functions and integrity levels: Safe Torque Off, safely limited speed, Performance Level, SIL. Those are the tools. They are not, by themselves, the reason a motor has to be designed a certain way. The reason comes from the application. Three papers in this year's source file make that unusually concrete, in three different markets.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: University and industry collaboration in electric motor research
posts.content:
Drive-safety practice is written in functions and integrity levels: Safe Torque Off, safely limited speed, Performance Level, SIL. Those are the tools. They are not, by themselves, the reason a motor has to be designed a certain way. The reason comes from the application. Three papers in this year's source file make that unusually concrete, in three different markets.

Aircraft: no single failure, and a very small number

In April 2021, Patrick R. Darmstadt and colleagues at Boeing, writing for NASA, assessed urban air mobility concept vehicles. The work was commissioned to guide industry and future regulation. The architectures they develop for distributed propulsion and flight control are intended to comply with EASA special condition SC-VTOL-01.

The authors call the most challenging criteria a catastrophic failure rate of no more than 10⁻⁹ catastrophic failures per flight hour, and the requirement that no single failure may result in a catastrophic event. They report that the aircraft evaluated may have paths to comply, but that stability-and-control models showed large power transients that must be addressed, and that preliminary system safety assessments show future work is needed in single-load-path structures, high-voltage power storage and distribution, and motor/rotor overspeed protection.

For an electric-machine engineer, the last item is the one that should not get lost. Motor and rotor overspeed is named as unfinished work, in a requirement set that already says a single failure must not be catastrophic. "The motor ran" is not the safety case. The drive and the machine are in the critical path for no-single-failure architecture, overspeed protection, and what happens to the power system when a unit fails.

That 10⁻⁹-per-flight-hour figure is a sourced aircraft criterion. It should be quoted as such. It should not be relabeled, rounded, or turned into a slogan.

Vehicles: the motor is inside the safety function

A 24 April 2025 paper by Mehmet Duran Menekşe and Mustafa Caner Aküner, in the Journal of Measurements in Engineering, examines design and functional-safety requirements for feedback motors in automotive steer-by-wire systems. Those systems replace the mechanical steering column with sensors, control units, and electric drives, and use a feedback motor to generate reactive torque for steering feel.

The paper emphasizes brushless DC motors for reliability and efficiency, and states that under ISO 26262 the failure rates of electric motors must align with the associated risk levels, and that the motors should incorporate safety mechanisms capable of detecting and isolating faults. In a snippet logged with the source, the authors also note that if redundancy is implemented, the design should consider a redundant item to switch to a backup motor if the primary feedback motor fails, and that scenarios where both motors fail should not be overlooked.

That is a different job description for a motor than torque, efficiency, and noise. The motor is part of the safety function. This post is about vehicle motion and by-wire actuation. It is not a claim about chargers; this source file does not contain an EV-charging safety paper.

Mobile robots: PLd, Category 2 or 3, and process safety time

A Texas Instruments technical white paper by Kristen Mogensen, Martin Staebler, and Ester Vicario, originally May 2023 and revised November 2026 (SPRAD98A), walks through a functional-safety assessment for a motor drive on an autonomous mobile robot. It uses ISO 3691-4 (industrial trucks / mobile robots) together with related Type C and drive standards such as ISO 10218 and IEC 61800-5-2. It explains Category 2 and Category 3 architectures under ISO 13849 (cited in the paper as IEC 13849-1), the relationship between SIL and Performance Level, and how device selection is tied to process safety time, with the aim of simplifying the assessment and potentially reducing bill-of-materials size and cost.

Robotics and AMR drive designers, in other words, are being asked to show PLd and Category 2 or 3 motor-drive safety, not just a working inverter. Process safety time is part of that choice, not an afterthought. Combined with the encoder argument from earlier in this series, the safety function again runs through the drive, the feedback, and the time in which a fault has to be detected and the machine put into a safe state.

EMS take

These three papers do not share a market, a voltage class, or a mechanical layout. They share a structure. The application writes a requirement (no single catastrophic failure, an ISO 26262 risk-aligned failure rate, a Performance Level and category). The motor and the drive then have to be designed, documented, and diagnosed as part of that function.

That is a different design problem from adding connected features in a crowded, low-margin application. It is also why Safe Torque Off, a second isolation barrier, and a justified encoder belong in the first half of this series, and why they are not the end of it. The numbers above do not tell you to bolt a second motor on the shaft. They tell you the machine, the inverter, and the feedback have to survive a defined fault, or the requirement is not met.

A later post will take the architectural half of that sentence: how FAULHABER, ABB, and an older NASA spacecraft paper all reject naive duplication in favor of redundancy designed into the machine.

All figures and claims in this post are from the cited sources. EMS is not announcing a product, a certification, a failure-rate target of its own, or a partnership.

posts.title: Do safe drive functions require safe encoders?
posts.excerpt: A drive that offers safely limited speed, or some other motion-safety function, is only as good as the signal that tells it how fast the shaft is turning. That sounds obvious. It is the part of the safety function that is easiest to leave as an assumption.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Diagram showing torque calculation for electric motor selection
posts.content:
A drive that offers safely limited speed, or some other motion-safety function, is only as good as the signal that tells it how fast the shaft is turning. That sounds obvious. It is the part of the safety function that is easiest to leave as an assumption.

In December 2013, Ralf Apfeld at IFA (the Institute for Occupational Safety and Health of the German Social Accident Insurance) asked a direct question: for a safely limited spindle speed function implemented at Performance Level d under EN ISO 13849-1, is a frequency converter with integrated SLS enough, or does the position and speed encoder subsystem also have to be a "safe" product?

The paper's conclusion is more careful than a yes or no. Conventional rotary encoders can be used in safety functions if it is demonstrated, in each case, that the required Performance Level is met. That generally needs manufacturer support and detailed product data. The fault exclusion for the mechanical coupling between the movement and the encoder is particularly critical on single-encoder systems. Using safe encoders is described as much simpler, because the necessary safety-related information is already available.

One technical detail from the paper is worth spelling out. A snippet logged with the source notes that if a check of the form sin²(φ) + cos²(φ) = 1 fails unnoticed, the next fault may lead to dangerous failure of the safety function, which is not permissible in Category 4, so further measures, such as redundant performance, are required. The lesson is not "always buy a safe encoder." It is that the encoder, the diagnostics, and the coupling are inside the safety function, and someone has to show the Performance Level for that whole chain.

What redundancy in the feedback path actually means

Trade and vendor writing in the same file is consistent with that, even when it is less formal than the IFA report.

A Control Engineering article on safety-certified and diverse-redundant encoders states a widely used method of keeping motion-control systems reliable: incorporate a degree of redundancy into the feedback loops, so the control system receives similar signals from two different sensors set up to measure the same thing. That is diverse or redundant sensing, not a second estimate inside a single un-checked channel.

Kollmorgen, writing about redundant servo feedback, describes a common OEM practice: specify a servo motor that already incorporates an encoder, and pair it with an external feedback device somewhere along the driven shaft or the load, so the second device can validate the first. That arrangement has a practical consequence the IFA paper would recognize. If both devices sit on the same mechanical path, a coupling or shaft failure can still be a common-cause problem. The second sensor only helps if its mounting and its failure modes are actually independent of the first.

A POSITAL white paper dated 23 April 2021 puts the detection requirement in plain language: for safety-critical applications, the motion-control system must be able to trust the position feedback it receives, and if a sensor malfunctions, the controller must be able to recognize the fault quickly and take appropriate action. Component failure, the paper says, can be detected more readily if the architecture is set up for that comparison. Again, this is a vendor technical note, not a standard, and it is cited here only for that detection point.

EMS take

Last week's STO discussion was about whether the drive can produce torque. This one is about whether the drive, or the safety controller, knows what the machine is actually doing.

Adding SLS, SOS, or another motion-safety function to a drive does not automatically make the feedback chain safe. Motor and drive engineers still have to justify the encoder architecture (one versus two, conventional versus safe) and the shaft coupling, or the Performance Level for the whole safety function will not hold. The IFA report is unusually clear about that, and it is unusually honest that a safe encoder is often the simpler path only because the data already exists.

If the machine is a robot, a medical table, a by-wire actuator, or any other place where unexpected motion is the hazard, this is not a purchasing footnote. It is part of designing redundancy, or at least diagnostic coverage, into the motor system rather than assuming the drive's safety function ends at the terminals.

The next question in this series is not "which encoder catalog." It is which applications are already writing the numbers that this feedback chain has to meet.

All figures and claims in this post are from the cited sources. EMS is not endorsing a specific encoder product or announcing a partnership.

(December 2013), https://www.dguv.de/medien/ifa/en/pub/rep/pdf/reports2013/ifar0713e/safe_drive_controls.pdf ; "Safety-certified and diverse-redundant encoders for motion control," Control Engineering, https://www.controleng.com/safety-certified-and-diverse-redundant-encoders-for-motion-control/ ; Kollmorgen, "Redundant Servo Feedback: When Fail-Safe Positioning Is a Must," https://www.kollmorgen.com/en-us/blogs/redundant-servo-feedback-when-fail-safe-positioning-must ; POSITAL, diverse-redundant encoder white paper (23 April 2021), https://www.posital.com/media/posital_media/documents/TCR_Divers-Redundant_Encoder_WHITEPAPER_2021-04-23.pdf

posts.title: STO is the floor, not the safety function
posts.excerpt: Safe Torque Off is easy to over-read. It is a real, standardized safety function, and it can replace a lot of iron in a cabinet. It is not, by itself, a safe machine, a safe process, or a redundant motor.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Electric motor efficiency classes IE1 through IE4 visualized for industrial buyers
posts.content:
Safe Torque Off is easy to over-read. It is a real, standardized safety function, and it can replace a lot of iron in a cabinet. It is not, by itself, a safe machine, a safe process, or a redundant motor.

The Control Techniques application guide (part 0704-0000-06, September 2020) is still a clear place to start. It describes STO as a built-in functional-safety feature, compliant with IEC 61800-5-2 / EN 61800-5-2, that disables the drive output so the drive cannot generate torque in the motor. Without a +24 V enable, the guide says, the drive is disabled to a high degree of integrity: no single component failure, and only very unlikely combinations of multiple failures, could result in it being enabled. In that role, STO can take the place of conventional contactors with cross-checked auxiliaries.

The same guide is explicit about the limit. Using an STO-capable drive does not, by itself, make a complete control system safe. The whole system still has to be designed to recognized safety principles. That sentence is the one worth keeping on the printout, because it is the one that gets dropped in product copy.

A 2020 Industrial Equipment News piece on motor-drive STO makes a related hardware point, and only that point is used here. Typical VFD STO reliability, it says, is improved by a degree of redundancy because the circuit is triggered by two separate inputs expecting normally closed circuits. The dual-channel input has tight tolerances for when those two circuits close, and a safety relay with a dual-channel output is recommended. Dual-channel STO inputs are a redundancy inside the stop function. They are not a second motor, and they are not a complete safety function for speed, position, or process trip.

Why process engineers are borrowing it

STO started as a drive function for machinery. It is now being read as a template in a different industry.

In 2025, Lotti, Maporti, Baumgaertl, Mocellin, and Pauletto discussed functional-safety challenges as fuel-fired process equipment is replaced by high-power electrical systems, including the need to de-energize those systems safely in an emergency (Chemical Engineering Transactions 116). Conventional safety relays and contactors, they report, create redundancy but lead to bulky, complex installations at large scale. As part of the EReTech project, a 250 kW electrified steam-methane reformer was built, and the authors found similarities between the control of electric-motor inverters and the thyristor control of an electrically heated reactor. They argue that the STO function commonly used in inverters could provide a reliable, more compact method for safely powering off those thyristors.

That is a serious compliment to drive-safety practice. It is also a reminder of the Control Techniques warning. If process plants start using STO language for high-power trips, they inherit the same obligation the machinery world already has: the stop function has to sit inside a designed safety function, with the rest of the architecture, the diagnostics, and the proof-test assumptions written down.

EMS take

For motor and drive engineers, STO is the right floor. If the hazard is unintended torque, a dual-channel, IEC 61800-5-2 function built into the drive is a cleaner starting point than a pair of contactors that someone has to wire, test, and keep in the safety chain. The CET paper shows why people outside the usual machine-builder audience are reaching for it: high-power electrification needs a compact, repeatable way to take energy out of the load.

The mistake is to stop there and call the product safe, or "redundant," because STO is present. STO answers "can this drive produce torque?" It does not answer whether the speed or position feedback is justified, whether the isolation barriers are in place, or whether a fault in the machine itself has a defined safe state. Those questions belong to later pieces in this series: encoders and coupling, IEC 61800-5-1 isolation, and what in-machine redundancy actually looks like when a second motor on the shaft is the wrong default.

If you specify or design motors for places where a failed trip costs health, life, or expensive equipment, treat STO as the entry condition. Then ask what else the safety function still has to do.

All figures and claims in this post are from the cited sources. EMS is not announcing a product, a certification, or a partnership.

posts.title: Motor Safety Roundup: June–November 2026
posts.excerpt: From 8 June through 25 November 2026, a daily monitor logged technical material on motor and drive safety, with a standing interest in redundancy. This post is a map of that file, dated today. It is not a claim that EMS published these papers, and it is not a backdated archive of posts that were never on the site.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Engineer inspecting a motor component on the bench
posts.content:
From 8 June through 25 November 2026, a daily monitor logged technical material on motor and drive safety, with a standing interest in redundancy. This post is a map of that file, dated today. It is not a claim that EMS published these papers, and it is not a backdated archive of posts that were never on the site.

The working inventory has 421 distinct articles after tracking-parameter normalization (429 raw "new result" mentions; one Texas Instruments isolation paper appeared nine times with different `ts=` query values). Those 421 figures are distinct URLs, not necessarily 421 distinct publications: a few works, including a 1987 NASA spacecraft-motor paper, show up under more than one NTRS path. Daily notes cover 169 of the 171 calendar days in the span; 18 June and 27 June have no file. Forty-three days exist but logged no net-new result. Original publication dates of the underlying papers are often missing from the notes. The dates below are when the monitor first saw the URL, unless a source date is stated from the paper itself.

What the file is actually full of

The monitor's own category tag is not very useful here. Most items were filed as "compliance / functional safety," which flattens the collection. Reading titles, URLs, and snippets instead, the largest multi-label clusters are:

  • STO and drive functional safety (IEC 61800-5-2, ISO 13849, SIL / PL): 238 articles
  • EV, traction, and automotive functional safety (including ISO 26262): 94
  • Encoders and position feedback: 43
  • Motor protection, overload, and arc flash: 37
  • Machine-level redundancy and fault tolerance (isolated phases, dual windings, dual inverters): 16
  • Aerospace and urban air mobility: 14
  • Robotics and AMRs: 13

Several clusters that a reader might expect are thin or empty. There is one distinct paper on IEC 61800-5-1 isolation (Texas Instruments SLYY080B, first seen 4 November, logged nine times). There is one strong process-industry electrification paper (Lotti et al., Chemical Engineering Transactions, 2025). There are no motor-safety recalls, accident reports, or enforcement actions in the 421 URLs. If you came looking for an incidents hook, it is not in this file.

ISO catalog pages for ISO 13849-1 (2015 and 2023 editions, plus a DIS for Part 2) were logged. Official ISO pages have been awkward public-link targets in earlier checks, so this roundup does not lean on them.

A few papers worth keeping on the desk

The point of a roundup is to point, not to rewrite every paper. A short list of primary or near-primary sources, for later reading:

  • Control Techniques, Safe Torque Off application guide (IEC 61800-5-2, 2020): https://cdn-static.nidec-netherlands.nl/media/4358-engineering-documentatie-safe-torque-off-guide-en-iss6-0704-0000.pdf
  • Ralf Apfeld, IFA / DGUV, Do safe drive controls also require safe position encoders? (2013): https://www.dguv.de/medien/ifa/en/pub/rep/pdf/reports2013/ifar0713e/safe_drive_controls.pdf
  • Anant S. Kamath, Texas Instruments, Isolation in AC Motor Drives (IEC 61800-5-1, SLYY080B, May 2026): https://www.ti.com/lit/wp/slyy080b/slyy080b.pdf
  • Kristen Mogensen, Martin Staebler, and Ester Vicario, Texas Instruments, Simplifying Robotics Motor Drive Safety Assessments (SPRAD98A, revised November 2026): https://www.ti.com/lit/wp/sprad98/sprad98.pdf
  • Mehmet Duran Menekşe and Mustafa Caner Aküner, Electric motor design for steer-by-wire systems and functional safety analysis (Extrica, 24 April 2025): https://www.extrica.com/article/24808
  • Patrick R. Darmstadt et al., Reliability and Safety Assessment of Urban Air Mobility Concept Vehicles (NASA/CR-20210017188, 2021): https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20210017188/downloads/1540_Boeing%20NASA:CR-20210017188_FINAL_013122.pdf
  • FAULHABER, Implementation of Redundancy in a Miniature Stepper Motor: https://www.faulhaber.com/en/know-how/tutorials/stepper-motor-tutorial-implementation-of-redundancy-in-a-miniature-stepper-motor/
  • H. Burzanowska, P. Sario, Ch. Stulz, and P. Joerg, ABB, Redundant Drive with DTC and Dual-Star Synchronous Machine (2007): https://library.e.abb.com/public/6ecce91d66ee4088a3dc05283cd59d82/Redundant_Drive_with_DTC_and_Dual-Star_Synchronous_Machine.pdf
  • Robert J. Smith and Alastair R. Flew, Redundancy for Electric Motors in Spacecraft Applications (NASA, 1987): https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19870006901/downloads/19870006901.pdf
  • Angela Lotti et al., Process Industry Undergoing Electrification (Chem. Eng. Trans. 116, 2025): https://www.cetjournal.it/cet/25/116/025.pdf

Vendor pages, forums, and syndicated trade posts make up a large share of the 421. They are in the inventory. They are not the spine of this list.

EMS take

The useful way to read six months of this file is not "smart motors are trending." It is that three engineering arguments keep repeating, at very different scales.

Stop functions, isolation, and a justified feedback chain are the floor. They are also easy to mistake for the finished safety function. STO in a drive, a second isolation barrier under IEC 61800-5-1, and a safe or redundant encoder are each necessary. None of them, by itself, is an in-machine redundancy story.

Where the application is EV, robotics, aerospace, or other work in which a loss of life, health, or expensive equipment matters, the requirement sets are already written (ISO 26262, ISO 3691-4 and related robot standards, EASA SC-VTOL-01). Those documents, not a marketing brief, are what set the numbers.

And when authors actually design for those numbers, they keep rejecting a naive spare motor. Isolated phases, dual windings with two inverters, or a deliberately chosen prime and redundant arrangement show up from a miniature stepper to a 1 MW ship drive to a spacecraft mechanism.

We will take those three arguments one at a time in December, on the real dates the posts go up.

This roundup summarizes a working inventory. It does not invent member counts, incident rates, or product claims. Further EMS posts in this series will cite the source papers in more detail.

posts.title: Two ways motor designers are engineering around dysprosium and terbium
posts.excerpt: China still restricts Dy, Tb, and Sm. Platts assessed Dy oxide at $4,100/kg on Oct 30. Here is how ZF and YASA are cutting heavy rare earths, and the questions that apply outside automotive.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Engineer inspecting a motor component on the bench
posts.content:
If you spec, design, or buy PM motors, the magnet line on your BOM got a lot less boring this year. The supply picture is easy to misread. The design responses are worth studying even if you never touch a traction drive.

The supply picture

On Nov 9, 2026, China's Ministry of Commerce extended the suspension of its October-announced export controls to Jan 10, 2027. That suspension covers holmium, erbium, thulium, europium, and ytterbium, plus some processing tech and equipment. It is not a pause on everything.

The April 2025 controls are a different story. Samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, and yttrium remain controlled. That matters because Dy and Tb are what keep NdFeB magnets from demagnetizing at high temperature. Sm is the "Sm" in SmCo. These are exactly the materials in the high-temp, high-coercivity grades used in traction, aerospace, and defense motors.

Prices reflect that split. Platts assessed dysprosium oxide (CIF North America) at $4,100/kg on Oct 30, 2026, versus $1,200/kg at the assessment's Mar 31 launch. Terbium oxide: $8,100/kg versus $4,900/kg. Those are dated assessments, not live quotes. Check current numbers before you use them in a bid.

The IEA estimates China held 61% of mined rare earth supply and 91% of refining and processing capacity for major rare earths in 2024 (cited by S&P Global).

A second date sits on the calendar for anyone in a defense supply chain: Jan 1, 2027, when tighter U.S. DFARS sourcing rules for NdFeB and SmCo magnets take effect.

Response 1: spin it faster

ZF announced a 3-in-1 drive on Nov 5, 2026 that runs up to 30,000 rpm. The logic is first-principles motor design: at the same power, higher speed means lower torque, and torque scales closely with rotor volume. Smaller rotor, less magnet.

ZF's numbers versus its 18,000 rpm SELECT drive: nearly 25% smaller, nearly 25% lighter, and 50% less magnet mass. The torque comes back through a two-stage helical gear set at about 18:1. The version shown: 200 kW peak, 3,500 Nm peak at the wheel.

The trade is real. NVH, bearing life, rotor retention, and gear design all get harder at 30,000 rpm. ZF says it treated motor, gearing, bearings, and tooth geometry as one system. That is the lesson worth taking: you do not get the magnet savings by optimizing the motor alone.

Response 2: change the magnet recipe, or drop it

YASA, the axial-flux motor company, received UK Government DRIVE35 grant funding for two parallel paths under Project Resilience. One path is heavy-rare-earth-free PM designs for high-performance BEV and hybrid applications, aiming to keep power density without adding mass or package size. The other is fully rare-earth-free axial flux motors for applications with different cost and performance targets.

One path cuts the heavy rare earths and keeps the magnet. The other drops the rare earth magnet entirely. Both are development programs, not production claims.

What this means if you are not an automotive OEM

Most Electric Motor Society readers work on industrial, HVAC, pump, appliance, and motion motors, not 200 kW traction drives. The same questions still apply:

  • Does your magnet grade actually need the Dy/Tb content it has, or did the spec carry over a thermal margin from an older design?
  • Could better cooling or a lower hot-spot temperature let you drop to a lower-coercivity grade?
  • For defense-adjacent work: do you know your magnet supply chain back to the mine before Jan 1, 2027?
  • Would a ferrite, induction, or synchronous reluctance design meet the duty cycle at an acceptable size and efficiency penalty?

We put those questions, plus supplier and grade checks, into a one-page Heavy Rare Earth Exposure Checklist.

If magnet cost or lead time changed a design decision on your bench this year, EMS is where that kind of field experience gets shared.

posts.title: Calculating Torque Requirements for Motor Selection
posts.excerpt: A detailed guide to determining torque requirements based on load characteristics and application needs, crucial for accurate motor sizing.
posts.content:
Calculating Torque Requirements for Motor Selection

Selecting the appropriate motor for any mechanical application hinges critically on understanding the torque requirements that the motor must meet. Torque calculation is foundational to motor sizing and ensures reliable performance, optimal efficiency, and longevity of the system. This article provides a structured approach to determining torque based on load characteristics and application demands, expanding on principles relevant to professionals referencing the Electric Motor Society’s guidelines.

Understanding Torque in Motor Applications

Torque represents the rotational force produced by a motor shaft and is typically measured in Newton-meters (Nm) or pound-feet (lb-ft). Accurately calculating the torque needed to drive a load is essential because underestimating torque can result in motor stalling or mechanical failure, while oversizing leads to higher initial costs and inefficiencies.

Torque requirements depend largely on load type, whether it’s constant, variable, or involves transient conditions such as startup or overloads. Distinguishing these load conditions is a critical first step.

Step 1: Load Analysis and Classification

Analyze the load characteristics in detail:

  • Steady Loads: Constant torque demand throughout operation, typical in conveyors or pumps.
  • Variable Loads: Changing torque, such as in machine tools or variable speed drives.
  • Inertia and Starting Loads: Consider loads with high inertia requiring additional torque during startup phases, e.g., crushers or mixers.

Documenting the torque profile over an entire operating cycle provides a comprehensive view of requirements.

Step 2: Calculating Required Shaft Torque

The fundamental formula for calculating torque ( au) is:

 au =  au_{load} +  au_{acceleration} +  au_{overloads}

  •  au_{load} — Torque needed to overcome friction and load resistance;
  •  au_{acceleration} — Torque to accelerate the inertial load (calculated by  au = J  d dt, where J is moment of inertia,  d dt angular acceleration);
  •  au_{overloads} — Additional torque for transient conditions or safety margins.

For rotational loads, calculate the moment of inertia (J) based on mass distribution and geometry. Then, estimate the acceleration torque by multiplying J by the angular acceleration required to reach operational speed.

Step 3: Incorporating Safety Margins and Application Factors

Electric Motor Society standards recommend applying a safety factor to the calculated torque to account for uncertainties such as variations in load conditions or unexpected torque spikes. Common practice includes multiplying the calculated maximum torque by a factor between 1.25 and 1.5, depending on application criticality.

Other selection criteria include:

  • Service factor—accounts for duty cycle variations.
  • Environmental conditions—temperature, humidity, and vibration may affect motor performance.
  • Motor starting method—impacting peak torque demands.

Step 4: Final Motor Sizing Based on Torque and Speed

Once the required torque is known, motor sizing involves pairing torque with the necessary speed (RPM). The power rating (P) can then be calculated from torque ( au) and angular velocity ( d) as:

P =  au imes  d

Where P is power (in watts if torque is in Nm and angular velocity in radians per second). Confirm the motor’s continuous and peak torque ratings match or exceed the calculated requirements.

Conclusion

Accurate torque calculation is indispensable for effective motor selection, ensuring system reliability and operational efficiency. By thoroughly analyzing load types, calculating shaft torque with appropriate safety margins, and matching motor performance to application demands, engineers can confidently select motors that meet the precise needs of their projects. For detailed standards and guidance, the Electric Motor Society remains a valuable resource for engineering professionals involved in motor sizing and selection tasks.

posts.title: NEMA Motor Sizing Standards Explained
posts.excerpt: A practical introduction to NEMA frame sizes, service factors, and how motor sizing decisions affect reliability and performance.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Technical overview of NEMA motor sizing standards and frame selection
posts.content:
Why sizing standards matter

Motor sizing is one of the most common sources of avoidable system problems. When a motor is oversized, energy efficiency and cost can suffer. When it is undersized, heat, premature wear, and poor performance usually follow. NEMA standards give engineers a common language for frame dimensions, mounting patterns, and performance expectations.

Frame size is not the whole story

A NEMA frame tells you a lot about shaft height, mounting geometry, and physical compatibility, but it does not replace a real load analysis. Torque requirements, starting conditions, ambient temperature, duty cycle, and service factor all still matter.

Where engineers get tripped up

  • Assuming nameplate horsepower alone is enough
  • Ignoring starting torque and overload conditions
  • Skipping enclosure and environment considerations
  • Overlooking how variable speed operation changes the thermal picture

A better workflow

Start with the mechanical load, confirm operating profile, then map those needs into a standards-based motor selection process. Standards help narrow the field, but application context finishes the job.

Why EMS cares

For the electric motor industry, standardization is what allows engineers, OEMs, and end users to collaborate efficiently. Better sizing decisions lead directly to better uptime, lower operating cost, and stronger trust in electric motor systems.

posts.title: Motor Efficiency Classes: IE1 Through IE4
posts.excerpt: A straightforward guide to international motor efficiency classes and what they mean for operating cost, compliance, and equipment strategy.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Electric motor efficiency classes IE1 through IE4 visualized for industrial buyers
posts.content:
Efficiency classes are becoming strategic

Efficiency classes used to feel like a compliance detail. Today they influence purchasing strategy, lifecycle cost, and sustainability reporting. As energy prices and operating expectations rise, the difference between a standard-efficiency motor and a premium-efficiency motor becomes economically meaningful.

What the classes mean

IE1 through IE4 provide a framework for comparing motor efficiency performance. Higher classes generally deliver lower electrical losses, but the right answer depends on duty cycle, run hours, load profile, and total installed cost.

When premium efficiency pays off

  • High run-time industrial applications
  • Systems with stable load and predictable demand
  • Facilities under energy reduction pressure
  • Applications where heat reduction improves reliability

Where caution is needed

Efficiency alone should not drive every selection. In some systems, control strategy, VFD integration, maintenance practices, or load matching produce more value than a simple class upgrade.

Bottom line

Efficiency classes are useful, but they work best when viewed as part of a full system decision. EMS sees this as a major area where practical education can help buyers make better long-term motor choices.

posts.title: How Electric Motors Shape Modern HVAC Performance
posts.excerpt: From ECM blowers to variable-speed control, electric motors now sit at the center of HVAC efficiency and comfort strategy.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Modern HVAC system using efficient electric motor control
posts.content:
HVAC is now a motor story

In many commercial and residential systems, HVAC performance is increasingly determined by motor and control quality rather than by simple equipment size alone. Variable-speed fans, electronically commutated motors, and smarter control loops have changed what building owners expect.

Why it matters

Comfort, acoustics, uptime, and energy cost all tie back to motor behavior. Better motor control means smoother airflow, fewer start-stop shocks, and better matching between system demand and actual output.

Where the gains come from

  • Lower part-load energy use
  • Improved comfort control
  • Reduced mechanical stress
  • Better diagnostic visibility

What engineers should watch

Not every HVAC upgrade is automatically efficient. Controls tuning, installation quality, harmonics, and maintenance still matter. The best results come from treating the motor as part of the full building-performance system.

EMS perspective

HVAC is one of the clearest examples of how electric motor expertise creates practical value in everyday infrastructure. It is exactly the kind of application area where the industry benefits from more shared knowledge.

posts.title: Motor Maintenance Schedules That Actually Work
posts.excerpt: Preventive maintenance is most effective when it is tied to operating reality, not generic calendar checklists.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Engineers reviewing electric motor maintenance and reliability planning
posts.content:
Calendar-based maintenance is not enough

Many maintenance teams still rely on fixed intervals that ignore operating load, environment, and actual condition. That usually creates one of two bad outcomes: unnecessary maintenance or missed failures.

What better schedules include

  • Duty cycle awareness
  • Temperature and vibration history
  • Lubrication discipline
  • Insulation and bearing condition checks
  • Environment-specific contamination controls

Why condition matters more than routine

A lightly loaded motor in a clean environment should not be treated the same way as a critical motor in a dusty, hot, or wet application. The maintenance schedule should reflect how the motor actually lives.

Where teams can start

Start with criticality ranking. Then align inspection depth and monitoring effort to the motors that carry the highest production or safety consequence. A small amount of prioritization usually produces a large jump in reliability.

Industry takeaway

Maintenance is not glamorous, but it remains one of the fastest ways to improve lifecycle value from electric motor assets. EMS wants to make that know-how more visible and more portable across the industry.

posts.title: The State of Electric Motors in 2026
posts.excerpt: An industry overview of electric motor technology trends, market growth, and emerging innovations shaping the future of electrification.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Electric motor industry trends 2026 showing market growth and EV motor technology
posts.content:
A Transformative Year for Electric Motors

2026 marks a pivotal year for the electric motor industry. Global electrification efforts, advancing battery technology, and increasing efficiency standards are driving unprecedented growth and innovation in motor technology.

Market Overview

The global electric motor market continues its strong growth trajectory:

  • Market size exceeding $180 billion globally
  • EV motor segment growing at 25%+ annually
  • Industrial motor efficiency upgrades driving replacement cycle
  • HVAC sector transitioning to high-efficiency motors

Key Technology Trends

1. Higher Power Density

Advances in materials and cooling systems are enabling motors that deliver more power in smaller packages. Silicon carbide (SiC) inverters and advanced thermal management are key enablers.

2. Integrated Motor-Drive Units

The integration of motors, inverters, and gearboxes into single units is reducing complexity, weight, and cost while improving efficiency.

3. Permanent Magnet Alternatives

Supply chain concerns around rare earth magnets are driving development of switched reluctance and induction motor alternatives that reduce or eliminate rare earth dependency.

4. Software-Defined Performance

Advanced control algorithms and over-the-air updates are enabling continuous motor performance optimization throughout the product lifecycle.

Looking Ahead

The electric motor industry is positioned for continued growth as electrification expands across transportation, industrial, and consumer applications. EMS is committed to supporting this growth through research collaboration, professional development, and industry networking.

Signals that matter

Why this matters for EMS

An industry in transition needs stronger coordination between manufacturers, researchers, integrators, and end users. The market story is not just about demand; it is also about whether the ecosystem can keep up with technical complexity.

What to watch next

Expect more attention on supply resilience, automation-driven motor applications, and education pathways that connect workforce development to advanced manufacturing and electrification.

Good research still needs a path to industry

Some of the most promising advances in electric motor design, controls, and manufacturing begin in research labs. But many ideas stall because they are not connected early enough to production realities, application constraints, or buyer needs.

Why partnership matters

The best partnerships are not just sponsorship logos. They include shared problem framing, practical test criteria, feedback loops, and real exposure to manufacturing and market constraints.

EMS role

EMS can help bridge the gap by making it easier for universities, sponsors, and practitioners to find each other around serious technical questions in motors and motion systems.

posts.title: ECM Motors: Efficiency and Control
posts.excerpt: Explore electronically commutated motors and how advanced control systems enable variable speed operation and energy savings.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: ECM electronically commutated motor efficiency and variable speed control for HVAC
posts.content:
Understanding ECM Motors

Electronically Commutated Motors (ECM) are a type of brushless DC motor specifically designed for high efficiency and variable speed operation. They incorporate advanced electronic controllers that optimize motor performance based on load and operating conditions.

Energy Efficiency Benefits

ECM motors can achieve efficiency levels of 80-90%, making them ideal for applications where energy consumption is a critical concern. The electronic control allows the motor to operate at optimal efficiency across a wide range of speeds and loads.

Variable Speed Control

Unlike traditional AC motors that operate at fixed speeds, ECM motors can vary their speed electronically. This enables:

  • Reduced energy consumption during partial load conditions
  • Better comfort control in HVAC applications
  • Extended motor life through reduced thermal stress
  • Quieter operation at lower speeds

Applications in HVAC

ECM motors are increasingly used in HVAC systems, where they can reduce energy consumption by 30-50% compared to traditional motors. The variable speed capability allows the system to modulate airflow based on actual heating or cooling demand.

Future Outlook

As energy efficiency regulations become stricter worldwide, ECM motor adoption is expected to accelerate. Manufacturers are continuously improving control algorithms and reducing costs to make these motors more accessible for various applications.

posts.title: Guide to Brushless DC Motors
posts.excerpt: Learn about BLDC motor technology, advantages, applications, and how they compare to traditional brushed motors.
posts.author: Electric Motor Society
posts.imageAlt: Brushless DC motor BLDC technology showing electronic commutation and efficiency
posts.content:
What are Brushless DC Motors?

Brushless DC (BLDC) motors are electric motors powered by direct current that use electronic commutation instead of mechanical brushes. They represent a significant advancement in motor technology, offering superior efficiency, reliability, and performance compared to traditional brushed motors.

Key Advantages of BLDC Motors

Higher Efficiency: BLDC motors typically achieve 85-90% efficiency compared to 75-80% for brushed motors, resulting in lower power consumption and reduced heat generation.

Longer Lifespan: Without brushes and commutators, BLDC motors have fewer wear components, leading to extended operational life and reduced maintenance requirements.

Better Performance: BLDC motors provide superior torque characteristics, faster acceleration, and smoother operation across a wide speed range.

Lower Noise: Electronic commutation eliminates the brush noise associated with traditional DC motors, making BLDC motors quieter and more suitable for noise-sensitive applications.

How BLDC Motors Work

BLDC motors use permanent magnets on the rotor and electromagnets on the stator. An electronic controller (ESC) switches the current flow to the stator windings based on rotor position feedback from Hall effect sensors or back-EMF sensing. This creates a rotating magnetic field that drives the rotor.

Applications

BLDC motors are used in a wide variety of applications including:

  • Electric vehicles and e-bikes
  • Drones and aerial systems
  • Industrial automation
  • HVAC systems
  • Power tools
  • Computer cooling fans
  • Medical equipment

Conclusion

BLDC motors represent the future of electric motor technology. Their superior efficiency, reliability, and performance make them the ideal choice for modern applications where energy efficiency and reliability are paramount.
